title: What makes a city and how cities began

hero.headline: From barley bowls in Uruk to 42 million people in Jakarta: what a city is and how the first ones began

prequestions.prompt: In 2025, what share of the world's people live in cities, using the UN's new global method (not counting towns)?
prequestions.explanation: 45%. Another 36% live in towns and only 19% in rural areas.

prequestions.prompt: Which is the world's most populous city by the UN's 2025 estimate?
prequestions.explanation: Jakarta, with about 42 million, ahead of Dhaka (37 million) and Tokyo (33 million).

prequestions.prompt: The earliest writing in Mesopotamia was mostly poetry and religious hymns.
prequestions.explanation: It was overwhelmingly accounting: barley, beer, sheep, workers. Literature came centuries later.

prequestions.prompt: How did people get into their houses at Çatalhöyük, around 7000 BCE?
prequestions.explanation: Through a hole in the roof, by ladder. There were no streets; people walked across the rooftops.

prequestions.prompt: India's 2011 census found 31% of people urban. Is the share of the world's town-dwellers who live in India and China together higher or lower than 30%?
prequestions.explanation: Higher: India and China hold more than 1.2 billion town dwellers, over 40% of the world total.

sections.title: A city that ran on bowls of barley
sections.intro_md:
Around **3100 BCE**, in the marshy south of what is now Iraq, roughly **40,000 to 50,000 people** lived inside one wall. Nothing like it had existed before. The place was **Uruk**, and its rubbish tells you how it worked.

Archaeologists digging there find the same crude clay bowl again and again, by the hundreds of thousands. It was pressed in a mould, thick-walled and ugly, and thrown away after use. The leading explanation is that it held a daily **ration of barley** for workers who no longer grew their own food. Nearby lie clay tablets with marks pressed into them: lists of barley, beer, sheep and labourers. One signs off with a name, **Kushim**, perhaps the first named person in history, and he was an accountant.

That is today's question in miniature. A city is not just a lot of people. It is a place where most people do not feed themselves, where strangers depend on strangers, and where someone has to keep the books. Today you will see where that began, how it spread on at least five continents, and why more than half of humanity now lives this way.

spotlights.name: Uruk, the first true city
spotlights.when: c. 5000 BCE founded; peak c. 3100 to 2800 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: Low, eroded mud-brick mounds in the desert near the Euphrates, now called Warka, ringed by the trace of a 9 km wall.
spotlights.story_md: Uruk grew from a village beside the Euphrates into a sprawl of about **250 hectares by 3100 BCE** and roughly **600 hectares by 2800 BCE**. Its wall ran about **9 km** and stood 12 to 15 m high. Two great temple districts, Eanna for the goddess Inanna and the terrace of the sky god Anu, sat at its heart. Here, between about 3500 and 3200 BCE, people began pressing signs into clay: the first writing. Many linguists think the very word **Iraq** descends from Uruk. UNESCO listed the site in **2016**. The river later moved away, and the city slowly emptied.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of a settlement crossing the line from big village to city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Uruk: the first place where strangers outnumbered neighbours.

spotlights.name: The bevelled-rim bowl
spotlights.spot_it: A coarse, thick, mould-made clay bowl with a slanting rim, found in heaps across the Uruk world.
spotlights.story_md: This is the most common pot of the Uruk period: at some sites it is the majority of all pottery found. It was made fast, in a mould or by pressing clay into a hole in the ground, and used once. One long-standing theory, put forward by the archaeologist Hans Nissen, is that it measured a standard daily **ration of barley or bread** handed to workers. The proto-cuneiform sign for 'to eat' or 'ration' looks like a head beside a bowl of this shape. Not everyone agrees; some think the bowls baked bread or moulded salt. Either way, a disposable, standardised dish points to something new: mass labour paid in food.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mass-produced tableware is a sign that a society now feeds people it does not know.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first city had paper cups.

spotlights.name: The Kushim tablets
spotlights.spot_it: Small clay tablets covered in pressed numerals and simple pictographs of grain, jars and people.
spotlights.story_md: One tablet from this period records **29,086 measures of barley over 37 months**, and is signed **Kushim**. Several tablets carry the same name, so Kushim may be the first person in history whose name we can read. He was not a king or a poet. He was an administrator, probably at a brewery or granary, counting barley in and out. (Some scholars think Kushim was a job title, not a person.) Early writing was overwhelmingly this: lists of rations, livestock, workers and debts. Literature came centuries later. The tablet shown here, from Jemdet Nasr in Iraq, is the same kind of record from the same era.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Writing was invented to run a city, not to tell stories.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first name in history belongs to an accountant counting beer barley.

sections.title: What counts as a city
sections.intro_md:
Ask ten countries what a city is and you get ten answers. **Denmark** and **Sweden** have called 200 people in close-packed houses an urban area. **Japan** has used 50,000. **India** uses a mix of law and numbers. The world's share of 'urban' people therefore depends heavily on whose ruler you use.

Scholars have tried for a century to pin the idea down. The sociologist **Louis Wirth** said a city is large, dense, permanent and full of different kinds of people. The archaeologist **V. Gordon Childe** gave ten traits, from full-time specialists to writing. In **2020** the UN Statistical Commission endorsed a single global yardstick, the **Degree of Urbanisation**, which simply counts people per square kilometre on a satellite grid.

Under that yardstick the UN's **World Urbanization Prospects 2025**, published in November 2025, found that **45%** of the world's 8.2 billion people live in cities, **36%** in towns and only **19%** in rural areas. National definitions added together say 58% urban. The gap is mostly Asia and Africa, including India, where millions live in places that look and work like towns but are counted as villages.

visual.title: The numbers that frame the day

spotlights.name: Size, density, difference: Wirth's city
spotlights.spot_it: Any street where you are surrounded by thousands of people you will never know, all doing different jobs.
spotlights.story_md: In 1938 the Chicago sociologist **Louis Wirth** wrote 'Urbanism as a Way of Life', still one of the most cited essays in the field. He defined the city as a **relatively large, dense and permanent settlement of socially heterogeneous individuals**. Each word does work. Size means you cannot know everyone. Density means you rub against them anyway. Heterogeneity means they are unlike you. From those three, Wirth argued, follow the city's habits: brief, polite, role-based encounters, money as the common language, weaker kinship ties and also more freedom and tolerance. Chandni Chowk in Old Delhi, shown here, is all three at once.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It defines a city by how people live, not by a legal boundary.
spotlights.memory_hook: Big, packed, mixed: if a place has all three, it is a city.

spotlights.name: The Degree of Urbanisation
spotlights.when: Endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission, March 2020
spotlights.spot_it: A map of the world cut into 1 km squares, each coloured by how many people live in it.
spotlights.story_md: The method was built by the EU, the OECD, the World Bank, FAO, ILO and UN-Habitat so that countries could finally be compared. Lay a grid of 1 km cells over satellite-based population maps. A **city** is a cluster of touching cells with at least **1,500 people per km²** adding up to at least **50,000** people. A **town** is a cluster of at least 300 per km² and 5,000 people. The rest is rural. No mayors, no laws, just people per square. Applied in **World Urbanization Prospects 2025**, it counts about **12,000 cities** worldwide. It also shows that much of South Asia is more urban than its own statistics say.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One ruler for the whole planet makes the urban world measurable for the first time.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1,500 per square kilometre and 50,000 in all: the UN's city in two numbers.

spotlights.name: India's census town
spotlights.when: Defined in the Census of India; 3,894 counted in 2011
spotlights.spot_it: A place with no municipality, often still called a village, where most men no longer farm.
spotlights.story_md: India counts two kinds of urban place. A **statutory town** has a municipal body notified by the state. A **census town** has none, but meets three tests: at least **5,000 people**, a density of at least **400 per km²**, and at least **75% of male main workers outside agriculture**. Their number jumped from **1,362 in 2001 to 3,894 in 2011**, and they accounted for about a third of urban growth in that decade, especially in West Bengal and Kerala. By these rules India was **31.2% urban in 2011**. Many census towns are still governed as villages by a gram panchayat, so they grow without town planning, drains or a municipal budget.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where India draws the urban line decides which places get city money and city services.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five thousand people, 400 per square kilometre, three in four men off the farm.

sections.title: Before the first cities: temples, towers and giant villages
sections.intro_md:
Cities did not appear out of nowhere. For about six thousand years before Uruk, people in West Asia and Europe experimented with living together in larger and larger groups, and each experiment broke an assumption.

At **Göbekli Tepe** in Turkey, people who had not yet fully settled into farming raised carved stone pillars around **9500 BCE**. At **Jericho**, a stone tower rose about **8000 BCE**. At **Çatalhöyük**, thousands of people lived in a honeycomb of houses with no streets at all. In Ukraine and Moldova, **Trypillia** villages swelled to 300 hectares around 4000 BCE, larger than early Uruk, then were burned and abandoned.

None of these is a city in Childe's or Wirth's sense: no writing, little sign of full-time specialists, no palaces. They are better described as **proto-urban**. They show that crowding together was possible long before it became permanent, and that something else, probably organised surplus and government, was needed to make it stick.

spotlights.name: Göbekli Tepe
spotlights.spot_it: Rings of T-shaped limestone pillars carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures on a hilltop near Şanlıurfa.
spotlights.story_md: When Klaus Schmidt began digging in 1995, he called it the world's first temple, built by hunter-gatherers before farming. That reversed the textbook order: perhaps ritual gatherings came first, and the need to feed the crowds pushed people to cultivate grain. Since Schmidt's death in 2014 the picture has shifted. Findings published in **2019** show houses, heavy grinding of cereals and rainwater cisterns holding at least **150 cubic metres**. So people may have lived there too. Geophysics suggests about **16 more enclosures** and nearly **200 pillars** remain buried. It became a UNESCO site in **2018**, with only about a tenth excavated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows large-scale cooperation and monument building before cities, and perhaps before farming.
spotlights.memory_hook: Temple first, village second, city much later.

spotlights.name: The Tower of Jericho
spotlights.spot_it: A squat, round stone tower 8.5 m tall, built against a town wall, with a staircase of 22 steps inside.
spotlights.story_md: Kathleen Kenyon uncovered it in the 1950s and showed that it, and the wall beside it, were Neolithic, about 5,000 years older than the biblical Joshua. For thousands of years it may have been the tallest building on Earth. Its builders used undressed stones; one estimate puts the work at about **11,000 working days**. It held no burials and probably was not a fort. In **2011** Ran Barkai and Roy Liran of Tel Aviv University showed that at sunset on the summer solstice, the shadow of a nearby mountain falls first on the tower and then spreads over the town. They argue it was built to awe people into living together.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the earliest public works: something a community built that no single family needed.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tower for a shadow: 11,000 days of work to make people feel like one town.

spotlights.name: Çatalhöyük, the town with no streets
spotlights.spot_it: Mud-brick houses packed wall to wall like cells in a comb, entered by ladder through a hole in the roof.
spotlights.story_md: There were no streets. People walked across the rooftops and climbed down ladders into their homes. They buried their dead under the floors and platforms where they slept, and painted the walls with bulls, vultures and hunters. One mural is often called the oldest map: houses with a twin-peaked volcano behind, though some think it is a leopard skin. Population estimates swing widely, from **600 to 800** people in an average year to **5,000 to 8,000** at the peak. Ian Hodder, who ran the dig from 1993, found little sign of chiefs, and diets and burials suggest men and women had similar status. UNESCO listed it in **2012**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves thousands of people could live packed together with no rulers, streets or writing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Front door in the ceiling, grandparents under the bed.

spotlights.name: The Trypillia mega-sites
spotlights.spot_it: Huge oval rings of thousands of two-storey clay houses on the Ukrainian steppe, known mostly from burnt remains and magnetic maps.
spotlights.story_md: Sites such as **Talianki**, **Maidanetske** and **Nebelivka** in central Ukraine covered up to about **335 hectares**, with as many as **3,000 houses**. Estimates for their people run from about 15,000 to more than 40,000, which would make them as large as early Sumerian cities and centuries older. Yet they had no palaces, no writing and few signs of rich and poor. Every 60 to 80 years settlements were deliberately **burned and rebuilt**, for reasons still argued over. A **2024** Kiel University study linked the mega-sites to low inequality, and their end to rising inequality a few generations later. They are the great 'almost city' of prehistory.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show that size alone does not make a city; organisation and permanence matter too.
spotlights.memory_hook: Europe's first megacity was a village that burned itself down every lifetime.

sections.title: Mesopotamia: the first urban world
sections.intro_md:
Southern Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, had almost nothing a city needs except two things: fertile silt and water. There was no stone, no metal and little timber. So everything had to be traded for, and to trade you need surplus, organisation and records.

By 2900 BCE the plain held a dozen rival **city-states**: Uruk, Ur, Eridu, Kish, Lagash, Nippur and more, each with its own god, temple, ruler and wall. Most people still farmed, but they farmed for the temple, the palace or a landlord, and were paid in rations. Specialists multiplied: scribes, priests, brewers, potters, metalworkers, soldiers, merchants who sailed to the Gulf and to the Indus.

The Sumerians themselves thought cities were the natural order of the world. Their **King List** begins: after kingship descended from heaven, it was in **Eridu**. For them, civilisation began when the gods built a city.

spotlights.name: The Warka Vase
spotlights.spot_it: A tall alabaster vase carved in bands: water at the bottom, then crops, sheep, naked men with baskets, and a goddess at the top.
spotlights.story_md: Found at Uruk in 1934, this vase of about a metre is one of the oldest narrative carvings in the world, and it reads like a diagram of a city's economy. At the bottom are water and plants. Above them march rams and ewes. Next come rows of identical naked men carrying baskets and jars of produce. At the top, the goddess Inanna, or her priestess, receives the offerings at her temple. Everything flows upward to the temple, which is exactly how Uruk worked. Looters stole it from the Iraq Museum in **April 2003**; it was returned two months later in pieces and restored.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a picture of surplus flowing from fields to a central institution, the engine of the first cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Read it bottom to top: water, wheat, sheep, workers, god.

spotlights.name: Gilgamesh and the walls of Uruk
spotlights.when: Stories from c. 2100 BCE; standard version c. 1200 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: A clay tablet of dense wedge-shaped writing; the best-known tablet tells the story of a great flood.
spotlights.story_md: The world's oldest great poem is a city poem. The Epic of Gilgamesh opens and closes by inviting the reader to climb Uruk's wall and look around: a square mile of city, a square mile of date groves, a square mile of clay pits, and the temple of Ishtar. Gilgamesh, a king who probably ruled around 2700 BCE, fails to win immortality. What he leaves behind is the wall. The message is striking for something so ancient: a person dies, but the city and its works endure. The real wall ran about **9 km**. The tablet pictured, in the British Museum, holds the epic's flood story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that by 2000 BCE people already saw the city itself as humanity's lasting achievement.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gilgamesh lost immortality but kept his wall.

spotlights.name: Ur and its ziggurat
spotlights.spot_it: A massive stepped brick platform rising from flat desert near Nasiriyah; in museums, a box inlaid with blue lapis showing war and peace.
spotlights.story_md: By about **2100 BCE** Ur may have held **100,000 people**, the largest city of its age. King Ur-Nammu built its great ziggurat, a solid brick mountain for the moon god Nanna, whose lower stage still stands. Leonard Woolley excavated the city from 1922 to 1934 and found the royal tombs, including Queen Puabi's gold headdress. He also found the **Standard of Ur** (c. 2600 BCE), a wooden box covered in shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli. One side shows an army with chariots; the other a banquet with farmers bringing animals and fish. The lapis came from Afghanistan, more than 2,000 km away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ur shows the full city package: king, god, army, specialists, and long-distance trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: War on one side, dinner on the other: the Standard of Ur is a city in two panels.

spotlights.name: Babylon and the Ishtar Gate
spotlights.spot_it: A gate of glazed blue bricks with yellow dragons and bulls in relief, now rebuilt in a Berlin museum.
spotlights.story_md: Babylon was a modest town until Hammurabi made it a capital around 1750 BCE. Its second golden age came under **Nebuchadnezzar II**, who rebuilt it around **575 BCE** with the Ishtar Gate, a processional way lined with glazed lions, and a ziggurat that may lie behind the Tower of Babel story. With perhaps **200,000 people** around 600 BCE, it was among the largest cities on Earth. German archaeologists excavated the gate between 1902 and 1914 and rebuilt it in the **Pergamon Museum** in Berlin from the original bricks. The ruins in Iraq became a UNESCO site in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Babylon became the West's lasting symbol of the great, sinful, glittering city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blue bricks, gold dragons, 200,000 people: Babylon was the New York of 600 BCE.

sections.title: Why people crowd together
sections.intro_md:
Living in a city was, for most of history, a bad deal for the body. Until the twentieth century many cities were so diseased that they needed constant migrants from the countryside just to hold their numbers. So why did people keep moving in?

The textbook story, from **V. Gordon Childe**, runs like this. Farming produced a **surplus**. Surplus could be stored, taxed and handed out. That let some people stop farming and become **specialists**. Specialists needed managers, managers needed **records**, records became writing. Writing was invented at least three times, in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and each time near cities with central stores. A ruling class grew around the store, and the store needed a wall.

Later research has complicated every step. Göbekli Tepe hints that gathering came before farming. Jane Jacobs argued that trade towns came first. And physicists have shown that cities obey strange mathematical laws: as they get bigger, each person becomes more productive and each road and pipe serves more people. A city is not just a pile of villages. It is a machine for multiplying contact.

spotlights.name: V. Gordon Childe and the 'urban revolution'
spotlights.spot_it: A gaunt Australian archaeologist in round glasses, author of the ten-point checklist for a city.
spotlights.story_md: Vere Gordon Childe, born in Sydney in 1892, became the most influential prehistorian of his age. In 1936 he coined the idea of an **'urban revolution'**, as important as the farming revolution before it. In a 1950 essay he listed **ten traits** of the first cities: large and dense size, full-time specialists, surplus handed to a god or king, monumental buildings, a ruling class, writing, exact sciences such as arithmetic and astronomy, sophisticated art, regular long-distance trade, and a state organised by residence rather than kinship. Archaeologists still argue with the list, but they still use it. Childe died in 1957 after a fall in the Blue Mountains, near his birthplace.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His checklist is still the starting point for deciding whether an ancient site was a city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten boxes: size, specialists, surplus, monuments, rulers, writing, science, art, trade, strangers.

spotlights.name: Surplus: the food that made strangers possible
spotlights.when: From c. 9000 BCE in West Asia
spotlights.spot_it: A field of wheat: cereal grain that can be harvested, dried, stored for years, measured and taxed.
spotlights.story_md: Cereals were the key. Wheat, barley and rice ripen at once, can be stored for a long time and can be measured in standard units. That makes them perfect for taxation and rations, in a way that roots or fruit are not. The political scientist James C. Scott argued that early states were in effect grain states, built where a taxable crop could be counted. A family farming silt in southern Mesopotamia could produce far more barley than it ate. Whoever controlled the extra could feed priests, soldiers and craftworkers. In the Indus cities, granary-like buildings and standard weights suggest the same logic.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without storable, countable surplus there are no specialists, and without specialists there is no city.
spotlights.memory_hook: No barley, no bureaucrats.

spotlights.name: The 15% rule: how cities scale
spotlights.spot_it: Double a city's population and wages, patents and crime per person all rise by about 15%, while pipes and petrol pumps per person fall.
spotlights.story_md: In **2007** Luís Bettencourt, Geoffrey West and colleagues compared hundreds of cities in the United States, Europe and China. They found power laws. Infrastructure such as road length, cables and petrol stations scales with an exponent of about **0.85**: a city twice as big needs only about 85% more. Social and economic outputs, such as wages, GDP, patents and also crime and some diseases, scale at about **1.15**: twice the people produce about 115% more. In plain words, every doubling makes each resident roughly 15% more productive and 15% cheaper to serve. West, a physicist from the Santa Fe Institute, compares it to biology, except that cities speed up as they grow while animals slow down.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why people keep flocking to big cities despite the cost and the crowding.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twice the people, 15% more of everything per head, good and bad.

sections.title: The Indus cities: drains, bricks and no palaces
sections.intro_md:
While Uruk and Ur rose, a second urban world grew along the **Indus** and the now-dry **Ghaggar-Hakra** rivers, across what is today Pakistan and north-west India. At its height, from about **2600 to 1900 BCE**, the Indus or Harappan civilisation covered more ground than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, with more than 1,000 known sites.

Its cities look strikingly modern. Streets ran roughly north-south and east-west. Houses had bathrooms and private wells. Covered drains lined the main streets. Bricks were made in a fixed **1:2:4** ratio from Gujarat to Punjab. Weights followed one system across a thousand kilometres.

What is missing is just as striking. No palace, no royal tomb, no grand temple, no statues of conquering kings. Whoever ran these cities did not advertise themselves. Their script, on thousands of tiny seals, is still undeciphered. India now holds most of the known sites, including **Dholavira**, **Lothal**, **Rakhigarhi** and **Kalibangan**, and they are the oldest cities in the subcontinent.

spotlights.name: Mohenjo-daro
spotlights.spot_it: Red-brick walls and lanes laid out in blocks, a stupa-topped citadel mound, and the rectangular Great Bath in Sindh.
spotlights.story_md: R. D. Banerji, an officer of the Archaeological Survey of India, recognised the site in **1919 to 1920**. Large digs under John Marshall followed from 1924. The city covered about **250 hectares** and held perhaps **40,000** people. It had more than **700 wells**, about one for every three houses, and covered drains along its main streets. The **Great Bath**, 12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.4 m deep, was sealed with a layer of bitumen to stop leaks. Its name means 'mound of the dead' in Sindhi. It became South Asia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in **1980**, and new excavation has been largely halted since 1965 to protect the fragile brick.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best-preserved large city of the Bronze Age and a model of public sanitation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven hundred wells and a bitumen-sealed bath, 4,500 years ago.

spotlights.name: Bricks in 1:2:4 and cubes of chert
spotlights.spot_it: Fired bricks with the same proportions everywhere, and small polished stone cubes used as weights.
spotlights.story_md: Across a region larger than Western Europe, Indus builders used bricks in the ratio **1:2:4** (thickness, width, length). A brick from Harappa matches one from Lothal 1,000 km away. Their **weights** were small cubes of chert, mostly in a binary series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) then in decimal steps, and so consistent that archaeologists can spot an Indus weight at sight. An ivory rule from Mohenjo-daro is marked in units of about **34 mm**, accurate to a fraction of a millimetre. Standards like these are invisible government: they mean trade, taxes and building codes worked the same in every city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shared standards are a sign of an integrated urban society, with or without a king.
spotlights.memory_hook: One brick, one weight, a thousand kilometres: the Indus ran on standards, not statues.

spotlights.name: Dholavira
spotlights.spot_it: Stone-walled city on an island in the white salt desert of Kutch, with huge rock-cut reservoirs and a ten-letter signboard.
spotlights.story_md: Locals call it **Kotada timba**. A villager, Shambhudan Gadhvi, drew officials to it in the 1960s; J. P. Joshi of the ASI recorded it in 1967 to 1968; R. S. Bisht excavated it from **1989 to 2005**. Built on **Khadir Bet** in the Great Rann of Kutch, where rain is scarce, the city lived on water engineering: at least **16 reservoirs** cut into rock and lined with stone, fed by two seasonal streams. Its plan has three parts: citadel, middle town and lower town. Near the north gate lay an inscription of **ten large Indus signs**, each about 37 cm high, once set on a wooden board: perhaps the world's oldest signboard. UNESCO listed it on **27 July 2021**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows an Indus city surviving in a desert by engineering every drop of water.
spotlights.memory_hook: A desert city that banked its rain and hung up a sign nobody can read.

spotlights.name: Lothal
spotlights.spot_it: A long rectangular brick basin beside a low mound near the Gulf of Khambhat, with drains and bead workshops nearby.
spotlights.story_md: S. R. Rao of the ASI found Lothal in **1954** and dug it until 1960. Its most famous feature is a large brick-lined basin, which Rao interpreted as a **tidal dockyard** connected to an old course of the Sabarmati, making it possibly the oldest dock in the world. Other archaeologists argue it was a water reservoir. Lothal was also an industrial town: workshops made carnelian beads that reached Mesopotamia, and a seal from the Persian Gulf was found there. The drainage, visible today, connected bathrooms to street sewers. India is building a **National Maritime Heritage Complex** next to the site.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Indus cities as trading ports linked to the wider Bronze Age world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dockyard or reservoir? Either way, Lothal plumbed its bathrooms into the street.

spotlights.name: Rakhigarhi
spotlights.spot_it: Eleven low mounds among wheat fields and village houses in Hisar district, Haryana.
spotlights.story_md: Rakhigarhi spreads over **11 mounds**. Before 2014 it was thought to cover 80 to 100 hectares. After new mounds were found, the ASI put the total at **300 to 350 hectares**, which would make it the largest known Harappan site, larger than Mohenjo-daro. Critics note that not all mounds were occupied at once. Only about **5%** has been dug. In **2019** a team led by Vasant Shinde published the first ancient genome from an Indus city, from a woman buried there. It showed no ancestry from the Central Asian steppe, a finding with big implications for debates about later migrations. In 2020 the government named it one of five 'iconic' archaeological sites.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It puts the largest Indus city, and the first Indus genome, inside India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rakhigarhi: a lost metropolis under a Haryana village, 95% still unexcavated.

spotlights.name: The 'Priest-King'
spotlights.spot_it: A small steatite bust of a bearded man with half-closed eyes, a headband and a robe patterned with trefoils.
spotlights.story_md: It is only **17.5 cm** tall, yet it is the most famous face of the Indus civilisation. Found at Mohenjo-daro in 1927, it is now in the National Museum of Pakistan in Karachi. The title 'Priest-King' was the excavators' guess, and a misleading one: there is **no evidence** that priests or kings ruled Indus cities. The trefoil pattern on the robe was once filled with red paste, and the headband has a disc at the front. Few human sculptures survive from these cities, which is itself telling: unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, the Indus elite did not cover their cities in portraits of rulers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the face we put on a civilisation that left almost no faces.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king in name only: the Indus had a sculpture called Priest-King and no evidence of either.

spotlights.name: The Dancing Girl
spotlights.spot_it: A slim bronze figure 10.5 cm tall, hand on hip, an arm covered in bangles, chin raised.
spotlights.story_md: Ernest Mackay found her at Mohenjo-daro in **1926**. She was cast by the **lost-wax** method, which means a wax model was covered in clay, melted out, and replaced with molten metal, a sophisticated technique for the time. She wears about two dozen bangles on her left arm and a few on her right, much as women in Kutch and Rajasthan do today. Mortimer Wheeler said there was nothing like her in the ancient world. After Partition she went to the **National Museum, New Delhi**, while the Priest-King went to Karachi, so the two most famous Indus objects now live in different countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows specialist metalworkers and a living Indian fashion, both at least 4,000 years old.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bangles to the shoulder, 4,000 years before the bazaar.

sections.title: Cities were invented more than once
sections.intro_md:
For a long time, scholars imagined a single cradle of cities in the Middle East, with the idea spreading outward. The evidence says otherwise. Cities arose **independently** in at least five or six regions: Mesopotamia, the Indus, China, the Andes, Mesoamerica and, later, parts of Africa. Each had different crops, gods and building materials, and yet they converged on similar answers: walls or boundaries, monuments, specialists, stores, and some way to keep records.

The differences are as instructive as the similarities. **Caral** in Peru had monumental pyramids but no pottery. **Teotihuacan** housed its people in apartment blocks. **Angkor** spread a low-density city across 1,000 km² of rice fields and canals. And in **2024**, laser scans from aircraft revealed cities in the **Amazon** that were 2,500 years old, in a forest once imagined as untouched wilderness.

There is more than one way to be a city.

data.records: Marks on jade and pots; script later

spotlights.name: Liangzhu, China's water city
spotlights.spot_it: Earthen city walls and a palace platform near Hangzhou, surrounded by rice paddies; in museums, square jade tubes called cong.
spotlights.story_md: Long before China's first dynasties, the Liangzhu culture built a walled city of about **290 hectares** in the Yangtze delta, with roughly **700 hectares** of planned settlement outside the walls. In the hills to the north they raised a system of earthen dams to control floods and store water, one of the oldest large-scale water engineering works in the world. The elite were buried with finely worked jade: discs called bi and square tubes called cong, the largest weighing 3.5 kg. Rice was the surplus; one store may have held about **15,000 kg** of grain. UNESCO inscribed the ruins on **6 July 2019** as evidence of an early state society in China.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It pushes China's urban story back a thousand years before the Shang dynasty.
spotlights.memory_hook: Liangzhu: dams, rice and jade, 5,000 years ago.

spotlights.name: Caral, the city that had no pottery
spotlights.spot_it: Stepped stone pyramids and sunken circular plazas in a dry valley 200 km north of Lima.
spotlights.story_md: When Ruth Shady began work here in **1994**, she found one of the oldest cities in the Americas, contemporary with Egypt's pyramids. About **3,000 people** lived in Caral, and some 20,000 across the Supe valley. The city has six large pyramid platforms and sunken round plazas, and it was built before the people of the region made pottery. Excavators have found **32 flutes** made of condor and pelican bones, and a knotted cord that may be an early **quipu**, the Andean record-keeping device. They have found no weapons, no defensive walls and no signs of battle. UNESCO listed the Sacred City of Caral-Supe in **2009**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a city built on ritual, trade and cooperation rather than war.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pyramids before pots, flutes instead of weapons.

spotlights.name: Teotihuacan, a city of apartment blocks
spotlights.spot_it: A long straight avenue running between giant stepped pyramids north-east of Mexico City.
spotlights.story_md: At its height, around **450 CE**, Teotihuacan probably housed about **100,000 people**, with estimates up to 150,000 or more, making it the largest city in the Americas and among the six largest in the world. Its **Pyramid of the Sun** stands about **65 m** tall. Most people lived in about **2,000 walled apartment compounds**, each holding 60 to 100 people. Whole neighbourhoods were migrant quarters: one, Tlailotlacan, was home to families from Oaxaca who kept their own pottery and burial customs for centuries. The name we use was given by the Aztecs, who found the ruins abandoned and called it the place where the gods were born. In **October 2025** researchers proposed a partial decipherment of its signs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a planned, multi-ethnic metropolis built without iron, wheels or draught animals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Teotihuacan: apartments, immigrants and a grid, 1,500 years before Manhattan.

spotlights.name: The garden cities of the Upano valley
spotlights.spot_it: Laser scans showing thousands of earth platforms joined by dead-straight roads under the Amazon forest of Ecuador.
spotlights.story_md: In **January 2024** a team led by Stéphen Rostain published in Science the results of a laser (LiDAR) survey flown over about **300 km²** of the Upano valley in eastern Ecuador. Under the trees lay about **6,000 rectangular platforms**, plazas, drainage canals, terraced fields and straight roads up to **25 km** long, linking at least 15 settlements. People began building around **500 BCE** and kept going for about a thousand years, growing maize, manioc and sweet potato in volcanic soil. Estimates of the population range from about 15,000 to 30,000 to well over 100,000. The authors call it 'garden urbanism': spread out, green, but planned.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It overturns the old idea that the Amazon could not support cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under the Amazon canopy: roads, plazas and 6,000 platforms, 2,500 years old.

spotlights.name: Angkor, the sprawling city
spotlights.spot_it: Stone temple towers rising from a moat in Cambodian forest, the centre of a vast web of canals and reservoirs.
spotlights.story_md: Angkor Wat is the famous temple, but the city around it was far bigger than anyone used to think. Studies using satellite images and, from 2012, airborne laser scans showed that roads, canals, rice fields and house mounds covered at least **1,000 km²**. That makes Greater Angkor the **largest pre-industrial city in the world by area**, though not by population. Estimates of its people range up to **750,000 to 1 million**. Its kings ran it as a 'hydraulic city', storing monsoon water in giant reservoirs called baray. Neglected waterworks, droughts, floods and war with Ayutthaya, which sacked it in **1431**, all played a part in its decline.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the model of a low-density, farm-filled city, a pattern found across the tropics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Angkor: a city you could not walk across in a day, mostly rice fields.

spotlights.name: Great Zimbabwe
spotlights.spot_it: Massive curving walls of fitted granite blocks with no mortar, and a tall solid conical tower inside the Great Enclosure.
spotlights.story_md: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a trading kingdom in southern Africa that exported gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean coast. Glass beads from India and Chinese porcelain have been found there. Its Great Enclosure has walls up to about **11 m** high built of granite blocks without mortar, the largest ancient structure south of the Sahara. The city may have held up to **18,000** people at its peak. Colonial writers and the white-minority government of Rhodesia insisted that Phoenicians or Arabs must have built it, and censored archaeologists who said otherwise. The site gave its name to the country of Zimbabwe at independence in **1980**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is African urbanism that colonial myth tried to erase, now a national symbol.
spotlights.memory_hook: Walls without mortar, gold from Zimbabwe, beads from India.

spotlights.name: Cahokia
spotlights.spot_it: A huge flat-topped earthen mound 30 m high rising over the Mississippi floodplain near St Louis.
spotlights.story_md: Around **1100 CE**, Cahokia in present-day Illinois held about **15,000 to 20,000** people, comparable to London at the same time. Its **Monks Mound** is about 30 m high and covers about 5.6 hectares at its base, the largest earthwork in North America north of Mexico. Rings of wooden posts, nicknamed Woodhenge, tracked the sunrise. Cahokia was the centre of the Mississippian culture, with plazas, more than 100 mounds and planned neighbourhoods. By 1350 it had emptied, possibly because of floods, drought, soil exhaustion and political breakdown. It became a UNESCO site in **1982**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a true city north of Mexico, centuries before European contact.
spotlights.memory_hook: London-sized, around 1100 CE, on the Mississippi.

sections.title: India's second cities: the Ganga plain
sections.intro_md:
After the Indus cities faded around 1900 BCE, South Asia went more than a thousand years without anything as big. Then, from about **600 BCE**, a second wave of cities rose on the Ganga plain. Historians call it the **second urbanisation**.

This time the cities grew out of the kingdoms called **mahajanapadas**. Iron tools cleared forest and ploughed heavy soils, rice paddies gave big surpluses, and punch-marked silver coins oiled trade. Buddhist and Jain texts are full of urban life: merchants, courtesans, guilds, moneylenders, gamblers. The Buddha preached in cities such as Rajagriha, Shravasti and Vaishali, and died near a small town, Kushinagar.

Rulers thought of cities as things to design and police: the **Arthashastra** lays out a fort city with three royal roads each way and twelve gates, and fines people for dumping dirt in the street. The greatest of these cities was **Pataliputra**, capital of the Mauryas, which a Greek ambassador described in astonished detail. Far to the south, digs at **Keeladi** near Madurai are showing an urban culture in Tamil country by at least the 6th to 3rd centuries BCE. India's urban story is not one beginning but at least two.

spotlights.name: The Cyclopean Wall of Rajgir
spotlights.when: Pre-Mauryan, c. 6th century BCE or earlier
spotlights.spot_it: Rough, unmortared boulder walls snaking along the hilltops around Rajgir in Bihar.
spotlights.story_md: Rajagriha, today's **Rajgir**, was the first capital of **Magadha**, the kingdom that would one day rule most of India. Its five hills were ringed by a wall of huge undressed stones, about **40 km** long, built without mortar. It is among the oldest stone fortifications in India. King Bimbisara, a contemporary and patron of the Buddha, ruled here, and Buddhist tradition places the First Buddhist Council in a cave nearby after the Buddha's death. The hills made a natural fortress, but the valley was cramped. Bimbisara's successors moved the capital north to the Ganga, to the site that became Pataliputra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marks the start of the Ganga plain's urban age and of the Magadhan state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty kilometres of boulders round five hills: Magadha's first fortress-city.

spotlights.name: Pataliputra
spotlights.when: Fortified c. 490 BCE; Mauryan capital c. 320 to 185 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: Lines of buried timber palisade beneath modern Patna, at the meeting of the Ganga and the Son.
spotlights.story_md: Ajatashatru fortified a village here around **490 BCE**, and his successor Udayin made it Magadha's capital. Under the Mauryas it became one of the largest cities in the world, with estimates of **150,000 to 400,000** people. The Greek envoy **Megasthenes**, who lived there around 300 BCE, described a city shaped like a parallelogram, guarded by a moat and a wooden wall with **570 towers and 64 gates**. Excavations since the 1890s at Bulandi Bagh have found long lines of massive **sal-wood palisade**, which matches his account. At Kumhrar, digs in 1912 to 1913 found the remains of a hall of **80 polished sandstone pillars**. By the time the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang came in 637 CE, the old city was mostly ruins. Modern **Patna** sits on top of it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the capital of India's first great empire and one of antiquity's megacities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hundred and seventy towers, 64 gates and a wall made of trees.

spotlights.name: Varanasi
spotlights.when: Settled at least c. 1000 BCE; claims much older
spotlights.spot_it: Steps of stone ghats descending into the Ganga, temple spires above, cremation fires at Manikarnika.
spotlights.story_md: Varanasi, or Kashi, is often called the **oldest living city in the world**. The claim is hard to test. Excavations at Rajghat on the city's northern edge show continuous settlement from about the early first millennium BCE, and nearby sites go back further, to the second millennium BCE. The Buddha gave his first sermon at **Sarnath**, a few kilometres away, around 528 BCE. Kashi was the capital of one of the sixteen mahajanapadas. What is beyond dispute is its continuity of purpose: for at least 2,500 years people have come here to bathe, study, trade silk and die. Several other cities, including Damascus, Byblos and Jericho, make the same 'oldest' claim.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best Indian example of a city held together by faith across millennia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Oldest? Unproven. Longest-running purpose? Very possibly.

spotlights.name: Keeladi
spotlights.spot_it: Excavated brick walls, ring wells and red-and-black pottery scratched with Tamil-Brahmi letters, in coconut groves near Madurai.
spotlights.story_md: Since **2015**, digs at **Keeladi** (Keezhadi) on the Vaigai river, first by the ASI under K. Amarnath Ramakrishna and from 2018 by the Tamil Nadu archaeology department, have uncovered brick buildings, drains, ring wells, dyeing vats and thousands of objects. Many pot shards carry names in **Tamil-Brahmi**, suggesting widespread literacy. Tamil Nadu has published dates from about the **6th century BCE**, which would make it contemporary with the Ganga plain's second urbanisation; others argue for later dates. The findings fit the urban world of Madurai described in Sangam poetry. In **2025** a public dispute broke out after the ASI asked for revisions to the excavation report.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It suggests that the south had its own early urban culture, not one copied from the north.
spotlights.memory_hook: Names scratched on pots: a literate town on the Vaigai 2,000 to 2,600 years ago.

sections.title: The giant cities of the old world
sections.intro_md:
For most of history, cities stayed small, because food had to be carried in by animals, carts or boats. A city of 100,000 was a marvel. Only a handful ever passed **one million** before the industrial age, and each needed an empire behind it to feed it.

**Rome** reached about a million around the start of the Common Era, fed by grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa. **Chang'an**, the Tang capital, a grid of 108 walled wards locked every night, reached a similar size around 700 CE, and **Baghdad** perhaps more around 1000 CE. Then came Hangzhou, Nanjing and Beijing. In South India, **Vijayanagara** may have held 500,000 people around 1500, second only to Beijing.

Every one of these cities shrank or collapsed when the system that fed it broke. Rome fell to perhaps 30,000 people in the early Middle Ages. Vijayanagara was sacked in 1565 and never resettled. Big cities are not just places. They are supply chains with people at the end.

visual.title: The world's largest city through time (estimated population, thousands)

spotlights.name: Imperial Rome
spotlights.spot_it: A vast plaster model of the ancient city, packed with temples, arenas and many-storeyed apartment blocks.
spotlights.story_md: At its height Rome probably held about **one million people**, the first city in the West to do so and the last until London around 1800. Most Romans did not live in villas. They lived in **insulae**, apartment blocks of brick and concrete up to six or seven storeys, with shops on the ground floor and the poorest families in the attics. Fires and collapses were so common that **Augustus** capped building height at about 70 Roman feet, roughly 21 m. Eleven aqueducts brought in water. A free monthly grain ration, the annona, fed about 200,000 citizens. When the empire split and the grain ships stopped, the population collapsed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rome proves a megacity can exist without engines, but only with an empire to feed it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A million people, six storeys high, living on free bread.

spotlights.name: Vijayanagara (Hampi)
spotlights.spot_it: Granite temples, bazaar colonnades and palace platforms scattered among giant boulders by the Tungabhadra river in Karnataka.
spotlights.story_md: Founded in **1336**, the capital of the Vijayanagara empire grew into one of the largest cities in the world. By **1500** it may have held around **500,000** people, second only to Beijing by some estimates, across a metropolitan area of about **650 km²**. The Portuguese traveller **Domingo Paes**, who came in about 1520, called it as large as Rome and very beautiful to see. Its bazaars sold horses, pearls and diamonds. After the empire's army lost the **Battle of Talikota in 1565**, the city was looted and burned for months and never resettled. The ruins at **Hampi** became a UNESCO site in **1986**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how quickly even a huge city can vanish when its state falls.
spotlights.memory_hook: As large as Rome in 1520, empty by 1567.

sections.title: The people who explained the city
sections.intro_md:
Every age has had someone trying to explain why cities exist and what they do to us. The questions barely change. Is the city natural or artificial? Does it make people better or worse? Why do cities rise and fall?

**Aristotle**, writing in the 4th century BCE, thought the city was the natural home of human beings. **Ibn Khaldun**, in 14th-century North Africa, saw cities as the late, luxurious and ultimately weak stage of a cycle that starts with tough desert tribes. In the twentieth century, Chicago sociologists such as **Louis Wirth** studied the city as a laboratory of human behaviour; **Lewis Mumford** wrote its grand history; and **Jane Jacobs**, a writer with no degree in planning, took on the planners and won.

Their ideas still shape what gets built, from mixed-use streets to fights against urban expressways.

spotlights.name: Aristotle and the polis
spotlights.spot_it: A marble head of a bearded Greek philosopher, copied by Romans from a bronze original.
spotlights.story_md: In his **Politics**, Aristotle wrote that the city (polis) comes into being for the sake of life, but exists for the sake of the **good life**. Families group into villages, villages into a city, and only in the city can humans fully use speech, law and justice. Hence his famous line that man is by nature a **political animal**, literally a creature of the polis. Anyone who can live without a city, he said, is either a beast or a god. He also had firm views on size: a city should be small enough that citizens know one another's character, and large enough to be self-sufficient. Athens, with perhaps 250,000 people, was already pushing it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the root of the Western idea that cities make us more fully human.
spotlights.memory_hook: Without a city, said Aristotle, you are a beast or a god.

spotlights.name: Ibn Khaldun's cycle of cities
spotlights.spot_it: A bust of a turbaned medieval scholar; he lived in Tunis, Fez, Granada and Cairo.
spotlights.story_md: Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis in **1332**, wrote the **Muqaddimah** as an introduction to a history of the world. In it he describes a cycle. Hardy nomadic peoples with strong group solidarity, **asabiyyah**, conquer settled lands and found dynasties and cities. City life brings wealth, specialised crafts, learning and luxury, but it also dissolves solidarity. After about three or four generations, roughly 120 years, the dynasty grows soft, taxes rise and a new tough group takes over. He also observed that big cities have more crafts and higher prices than small ones, an early theory of urban economies. He is often called a founder of sociology.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the first theories of why cities and states rise and decay.
spotlights.memory_hook: Desert toughens, city softens, the cycle turns every 120 years.

spotlights.name: Jane Jacobs
spotlights.when: The Death and Life of Great American Cities, 1961
spotlights.spot_it: A woman with a grey bob and big glasses at a 1961 press meeting, fighting a highway through Greenwich Village.
spotlights.story_md: Jane Jacobs (1916 to 2006) was a journalist living in Greenwich Village, New York. In 1961 she published **The Death and Life of Great American Cities**, an attack on modernist planning, slum clearance and towers in parks. Safe, lively streets, she argued, need short blocks, mixed uses, old buildings alongside new ones, and enough density. Shopkeepers and residents provide **'eyes on the street'**. She led the fight against the planner Robert Moses, stopping a road through Washington Square Park and the Lower Manhattan Expressway; she was arrested at a 1968 hearing. She then moved to Toronto and helped stop the Spadina Expressway there. In **The Economy of Cities** (1969) she went further, arguing through an imaginary trading town called New Obsidian that cities came before farming. Archaeologists reject that timeline.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Her ideas about mixed, walkable streets now guide planners worldwide.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eyes on the street beat cops on the corner.

sections.title: Planned or grown: India's designed cities
sections.intro_md:
Cities come in two broad kinds. **Grown** cities, like old Varanasi, Old Delhi's lanes or medieval Fez, take shape slowly through millions of small decisions. **Planned** cities are drawn first and built second, usually by a ruler or a government in a hurry: Chang'an, Jaipur, Washington DC, Brasília, Chandigarh.

India has an unusually long line of planned cities. Indus builders laid out grids. Kautilya wrote rules. Mughal emperors founded **Fatehpur Sikri**, abandoned about 14 years after 1571, and **Shahjahanabad**. A Rajput king and a Bengali scholar designed **Jaipur** by the shastras. Newly independent India hired **Le Corbusier** for Chandigarh. Today, **Amaravati**, Navi Mumbai, GIFT City and Dholera continue the habit.

Each planned city is a statement about power and about the future. Each also shows the limits of planning. People keep doing what the plan did not expect: settling informally, opening shops in houses, turning roundabouts into markets. The best planned cities leave room for that; the worst fight it.

rows.Chandigarh (1951): Numbered sectors with their own services

spotlights.name: Shahjahanabad and Chandni Chowk
spotlights.spot_it: A broad bazaar street running west from the Red Fort, crowded with rickshaws, sweet shops and hanging wires.
spotlights.story_md: Shah Jahan moved the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi and built a new walled city, **Shahjahanabad**, with the Red Fort at its edge, between 1639 and 1648. Its main avenue, **Chandni Chowk**, was designed by his daughter **Jahanara**. Down its centre ran a canal fed by the Yamuna, and a pool reflected the moonlight, which may be the origin of its name. Felice Beato's photograph of **1858**, taken just after the uprising of 1857, shows a wide, quiet street. Today it is one of the densest markets in Asia. A 2021 redevelopment pedestrianised much of the road between the Red Fort and Fatehpuri Masjid.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a planned Mughal capital that grew into a classic 'organic' Indian bazaar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Moonlight on a canal, then 400 years of shopping.

spotlights.name: Jaipur, the city of nine squares
spotlights.spot_it: Wide straight bazaars of pink-washed shopfronts meeting at right angles, with the latticed Hawa Mahal facing the street.
spotlights.story_md: Sawai Jai Singh II, a king with a passion for astronomy, founded Jaipur in **1727** and named it after himself. His architect, the Bengali scholar **Vidyadhar Bhattacharya**, laid it out using the **Vastu** and **Shilpa Shastra** principles: a grid of **nine blocks**, two for the palace and state, seven for the public, with broad market streets and walls pierced by seven gates. Each bazaar was given to a trade. The famous pink came later, in **1876**, when the city was painted to welcome the Prince of Wales. The walled city joined UNESCO's list on **6 July 2019**, praised as a rare planned trading city of its era.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's best example of a pre-modern city planned by traditional Indian design rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine squares and a coat of pink paint.

spotlights.name: Chandigarh
spotlights.spot_it: Raw concrete government buildings with sweeping roofs, and a city of rectangular numbered sectors between green belts.
spotlights.story_md: Partition in 1947 left Indian Punjab without a capital, because Lahore went to Pakistan. Nehru wanted a new city **'unfettered by the traditions of the past'**. The American planner **Albert Mayer** drew a curved plan, but his architect partner Matthew Nowicki died in a plane crash in 1950. **Le Corbusier** arrived in February 1951 and straightened Mayer's layout into a grid of self-contained **sectors**, each with its own shops, schools and green space, and designed the Capitol Complex. Its buildings became part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing in **2016**. Chandigarh is admired for its greenery and order and criticised for being built for cars and for pushing poorer workers to its edges.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is independent India's most famous attempt to build modernity from scratch.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city drawn on a blank sheet, numbered like a spreadsheet.

compare.difference: Both are grid cities built by rulers in a hurry. Jaipur followed the shastras and organised streets around trades; Chandigarh followed modernism and organised them around sectors and traffic.

sections.title: How urban is India, really?
sections.intro_md:
On paper, India is a rural country. The **2011 census** counted **31.2%** of people as urban, about **377 million**. That census is still the latest, because the 2021 count was postponed; the next one is under way now.

But the official number undercounts. India's legal line for 'town' is strict, and states have reasons to keep places rural, since villages receive rural development funds and are not taxed like towns. The UN's 2025 report, using its global grid method, finds that in India, as in Germany and the United States, **towns** are the most common kind of place people live, and that India and China together hold more than **1.2 billion** town dwellers. Independent studies using satellite and density data have long suggested that more than half of India already lives in urban-like conditions.

India also has some of the biggest cities on Earth. The UN counts **Delhi** at about **30 million**, fourth in the world, and **Kolkata** at about **22.5 million**. And over half of the world's projected 986 million new city dwellers by 2050 will be in just seven countries, India first among them.

spotlights.name: Two answers to one question
spotlights.spot_it: The same country, measured two ways: 31% urban by its own census, far more by satellite density.
spotlights.story_md: The difference comes down to definitions. A settlement of 20,000 people living at city-like density, with most men working in shops, workshops and transport, might still be a **village** in India's books if the state never notified a municipality and its male workforce does not quite clear the 75% non-farm test. Under the UN's **Degree of Urbanisation** it would be a town, perhaps even a city. The UN's 2025 report says national definitions add up to **58% urban** worldwide, while its grid method gives **81%** in cities and towns combined, and that the biggest gaps are in Central and Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. The practical question is money: towns need drains, waste collection and planning that panchayats cannot fund.
spotlights.why_it_matters: How we count decides which places get urban services and which grow without them.
spotlights.memory_hook: India is a village on paper and a town on the satellite map.

spotlights.name: The Mumbai local train
spotlights.spot_it: Packed blue-and-yellow commuter trains with open doors, passengers hanging out, running north-south down a narrow island city.
spotlights.story_md: Mumbai is a long, thin peninsula, and its suburban railway is its spine. The network carries about **7.5 million passengers a day**, more than the entire population of many countries. At peak hours a nine-car train built for under 2,000 people can carry more than twice that. This is density in action: only a railway can move that many people along a narrow strip of land. It also has a dark side. Hundreds of people die on the tracks each year, falling from crowded doors or crossing lines. The first passenger train in India ran here, from Bori Bunder to Thane, on **16 April 1853**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a city's shape and its transport decide each other.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven and a half million people a day through one narrow island.

spotlights.name: Dharavi
spotlights.spot_it: Low-rise roofs packed tight between railway lines in central Mumbai, full of workshops for leather, pottery, garments and recycling.
spotlights.story_md: Dharavi covers about **2.1 km²** in the middle of Mumbai and is home to an estimated **700,000 to 1 million** people, among the highest densities on Earth. It is often called Asia's largest slum, but it is also a factory district: thousands of small units tan leather, make pottery, stitch garments, print packaging and recycle plastic, with an informal output often estimated in hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Many families have lived there for generations, since the area was a fishing village in a marsh. In **2022** the Adani Group won the tender to redevelop it, a project that will decide who gets new flats and who must leave.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the informal city: dense, productive and unplanned, which is how much of the world actually lives.

sections.title: The age of megacities
sections.intro_md:
In **1975** there were eight cities of 10 million people or more. In **2025** the UN counts **33**, 19 of them in Asia, and expects 37 by 2050. Tokyo, the largest city on Earth for half a century, has been overtaken. Under the UN's new method, **Jakarta** now leads with about 42 million people, followed by **Dhaka** and Tokyo.

Megacities grab headlines, but they are not where most urban people live. Of the world's roughly **12,000 cities**, 96% have fewer than a million people and 81% have fewer than 250,000. Many of the fastest-growing places are these smaller cities in Africa and South Asia, which often have the least money and planning capacity.

Cities are also spreading faster than they are filling up. Between 1975 and 2025 the built-up area per person rose from **43 to 63 m²**, and about **60%** of land turned urban since 1970 was productive farmland. Meanwhile more than **3,000 cities**, 17% of them in India, actually lost people between 2015 and 2025.

spotlights.name: Jakarta
spotlights.when: World's largest city by UN 2025 estimate
spotlights.spot_it: A forest of towers rising from a flat coastal plain on Java, with endless traffic and grey sea walls on the north shore.
spotlights.story_md: Under the UN's 2025 method, the Jakarta urban area holds about **41.9 million people**, more than Canada. It is also one of the fastest-sinking cities in the world. Decades of pumping groundwater have made parts of North Jakarta sink by up to about **25 cm a year**, and much of the city lies below sea level behind walls. Floods are routine. In 2019 the government announced it would move the national capital to a new city, **Nusantara**, in Borneo. Jakarta will stay Indonesia's economic heart regardless. Its story shows that a city can be both the biggest on Earth and physically unstable underfoot.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest example of the risks of megacity growth on a vulnerable coast.

spotlights.name: Dhaka
spotlights.when: Expected to be the world's largest city by 2050
spotlights.spot_it: Rivers of cycle rickshaws, buses and people in a low-lying delta city, with garment factories at its edges.
spotlights.story_md: Dhaka, capital of Bangladesh, is second in the world with about **36.6 million** people by the UN's 2025 estimate, and is projected to become the **largest city on Earth by 2050**. It is among the most densely packed big cities anywhere. Much of its growth comes from rural migrants, many pushed by river erosion, floods and cyclones in a delta that sits barely above sea level, and pulled by jobs in the garment industry, which makes Bangladesh one of the world's biggest clothing exporters. Its traffic is legendary: cycle rickshaws, once counted in the hundreds of thousands, still fill the streets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows where the future of urban growth lies: South Asian deltas under climate stress.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dhaka: tomorrow's biggest city, built on a floodplain.

spotlights.name: Tokyo
spotlights.spot_it: Seas of mid-rise buildings, glowing signs and precisely timed trains; pedestrians streaming across the Shibuya scramble.
spotlights.story_md: Tokyo was the world's largest city from about **1965** until the UN's 2025 update put it third, at about **33.4 million**. Its fall in rank is partly a change of method and partly real: Japan's population is shrinking and ageing, and the UN projects Tokyo will drop to **seventh by 2050**. Yet Tokyo remains a model of how a giant city can work. It has one of the world's busiest rail systems, low crime, and surprisingly affordable housing for a megacity, because national zoning rules make it easy to build. It was rebuilt twice in a single lifetime: after the 1923 Kanto earthquake and after the firebombing of 1945.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that megacities can be safe, efficient and liveable, and that even giants eventually shrink.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tokyo: number one for 60 years, now gracefully getting smaller.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Cities attract legends. Some come from national pride, some from old textbooks, and some from the fact that the past is far harder to measure than it looks. Here are three ideas you will hear often, tested against what the evidence now supports.

The common thread: early cities were more varied, more widespread and more surprising than the simple story of a single cradle in the Middle East, from which civilisation marched outward. And modern cities are less dominated by giants than the headlines suggest.

spotlights.name: Myth: we know which city is the oldest
spotlights.spot_it: Any brochure that says 'oldest continuously inhabited city in the world'.
spotlights.story_md: Jericho, Damascus, Byblos, Aleppo, Argos, Varanasi and others all claim the title. The trouble is twofold. First, 'city' needs a definition: Jericho around 8000 BCE was a walled settlement of perhaps 1,000 to 2,000 people, impressive but not a city by Childe's standard. Second, 'continuously' is rarely provable; most sites have gaps of decades or centuries in their layers. The fairest statements are narrower. **Uruk** is the best candidate for the first true city. **Jericho** has some of the oldest town walls. **Varanasi** is among the oldest Indian cities still alive. Each is true without needing the superlative.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Good history depends on clear definitions, not slogans.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every 'oldest city' is the oldest something, never simply the oldest.

spotlights.name: Myth: most city people live in megacities
spotlights.spot_it: Any headline implying that urbanisation means Mumbai, Lagos and Jakarta.
spotlights.story_md: Megacities are dramatic but they are not typical. The UN's 2025 report is explicit: most of the world's city dwellers live in **small and medium-sized cities**. Of about 12,000 cities, **96%** have under a million people. In India the story is similar: much of the growth is in towns and census towns, places like Ludhiana's outskirts or the bazaar towns of Bihar, not only in Delhi and Mumbai. This matters for policy. Smaller cities often have the least money and the fewest planners, yet they are where most of the next billion urban people will live.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It changes where money, planning and attention should go.
spotlights.memory_hook: The urban future is a town of 100,000 you have never heard of.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The study of cities is changing fast, for two reasons. On the ground and from the air, new tools such as **LiDAR** and ancient DNA keep revealing cities nobody knew existed, or showing that known ones were bigger and older. And in the present, governments are counting and building cities on a scale never seen before.

The timeline below dates the main events. Three stories matter most for India and its neighbours: the census, a new state capital and a new national capital next door.

spotlights.spot_it: Enumerators with phone apps and an online portal where households fill in their own details.
spotlights.story_md: India's census, last held in **2011**, was due in 2021 but was postponed during the COVID-19 pandemic and then repeatedly delayed. The **house-listing and housing census** finally ran from **1 April to 30 September 2026**, state by state, with a 15-day window for families to self-enumerate online before the enumerator called. Population enumeration is set for **9 to 28 February 2027** (with snow-bound areas counted in September 2026). It will record each person's caste, the first full caste count since **1931**. The results will redraw India's urban map, deciding how many new census towns exist after 16 years of growth. Provisional figures are expected in late 2027.

spotlights.story_md: When Andhra Pradesh and Telangana split in 2014, Hyderabad went to Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh needed a new capital. The state chose a site on the Krishna and pooled about **33,700 acres** of farmland from the villages there. Work stalled from 2019 to 2024 when a new government proposed three capitals instead. It restarted in **June 2024**. In **April 2026** Parliament passed an amendment to the 2014 Reorganisation Act stating that Amaravati shall be the new capital. The plan includes a 195 km outer ring road and a 'Quantum Valley' tech park, with Phase I infrastructure targeted for **2028**. The name honours the ancient Buddhist town of Amaravati nearby.

spotlights.story_md: Indonesia is building a new capital, **Nusantara**, about 1,200 km from sinking, congested Jakarta. The site covers about **2,560 km²** in East Kalimantan, and the full plan, in five phases to **2045**, is costed at about **Rp 523 trillion**, roughly US$35 billion. A move planned for August 2024 did not happen; that year's Independence Day ceremony was held there with a reduced guest list. President Prabowo Subianto has kept the project going as a 'political capital', hoping to host a national assembly session there in 2028. The Vice-Presidential Palace was completed in **January 2026**. About 147,000 people lived in the area in 2025, mostly in older villages.

sections.title: Recap: what makes a city
sections.intro_md:
A city is not simply a big place. It is a settlement that is **large, dense, permanent and mixed**, where most people do not grow their own food and must trust strangers. That requires surplus, specialists, records and some kind of authority.

The first true city was **Uruk**, around 3100 BCE, with 40,000 to 50,000 people, bowls for barley rations and accountants who invented writing. Before it came temples, towers and giant villages, from Göbekli Tepe to Çatalhöyük to Trypillia. Cities were invented again, independently, along the **Indus** (Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi), in China (Liangzhu), in Peru (Caral), in Mexico (Teotihuacan) and even in the **Amazon**.

India's urban story has at least two beginnings: the Indus cities and the Ganga plain, with **Pataliputra** at its peak.

Today **45%** of humanity lives in cities and 36% in towns. There are **33 megacities**, Jakarta the largest. India counts itself 31% urban, but by global measures it is far more, and its 2027 census will show by how much.

best_facts.fact: The oldest personal name we can read may belong to Kushim, an Uruk-era accountant who signed a tablet recording 29,086 measures of barley over 37 months.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first name in history is not a king's but a bookkeeper's.

best_facts.fact: At Çatalhöyük, around 7000 BCE, there were no streets: people walked over the rooftops and entered their homes by ladder through the ceiling.
best_facts.why_surprising: A town of thousands with no streets at all.

best_facts.fact: Under the UN's 2025 figures, Jakarta, not Tokyo, is the world's largest city, with about 42 million people, and Dhaka is expected to take the top spot by 2050.
best_facts.why_surprising: Tokyo held the title for about 60 years.

best_facts.fact: In 2024 airborne lasers revealed about 6,000 platforms and roads up to 25 km long under the Amazon forest in Ecuador, built from about 500 BCE.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'untouched' rainforest was once an urban landscape.

best_facts.fact: Double a city's population and its wages, patents and crime per person each rise by about 15%, while it needs about 15% less road and pipe per person.
best_facts.why_surprising: Cities follow mathematical laws almost like organisms.

best_facts.fact: Mohenjo-daro had more than 700 wells, roughly one for every three houses, around 2500 BCE.
best_facts.why_surprising: Better household water access than many cities had 4,000 years later.

best_facts.fact: The Indus cities, spread over a thousand kilometres, used bricks in the same 1:2:4 ratio and the same weights, yet show no palaces or royal tombs.
Megasthenes described Pataliputra's wooden wall as having 570 towers and 64 gates; excavations in Patna have found long lines of sal-wood palisade.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of antiquity's great capitals was walled in timber.

best_facts.fact: Caral in Peru built pyramids around 2600 BCE, before its people made pottery, and excavators have found 32 bone flutes but no weapons.
best_facts.why_surprising: Monuments before pots, music instead of war.

best_facts.fact: Under its own census rules India was 31% urban in 2011, but the UN finds towns are the most common place Indians live, and India and China hold over 1.2 billion town dwellers.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'village country' is largely a town country.

best_facts.fact: Greater Angkor covered at least 1,000 km², making it the largest pre-industrial city in the world by area.
best_facts.why_surprising: Larger in extent than many modern capitals.

best_facts.fact: The Tower of Jericho, built about 8000 BCE, took an estimated 11,000 working days, and at summer-solstice sunset a mountain's shadow falls first on it, then over the town.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Stone Age public work possibly built around a shadow.

best_facts.fact: Jaipur was not pink when founded in 1727; it was painted in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales.
best_facts.why_surprising: The Pink City's colour is 150 years younger than the city.

best_facts.fact: Of the world's roughly 12,000 cities, 96% have fewer than a million people; most city dwellers live in small and medium-sized cities.
Trypillia mega-sites in Ukraine reached about 335 hectares around 4000 BCE, as big as early Sumerian cities, and were burned and rebuilt every 60 to 80 years.
best_facts.why_surprising: Europe had giant settlements before Mesopotamia's first cities.

side_dish.title: Why a city is not an elephant
side_dish.body_md:
Geoffrey West came to cities from biology. In the 1990s he and two ecologists, James Brown and Brian Enquist, explained one of biology's oldest puzzles: **Kleiber's law**. An animal's metabolic rate rises with its body mass raised to the power of about **three quarters**. An elephant is 10,000 times heavier than a mouse but uses only about 1,000 times more energy. Big animals are efficient. They also live slower: their hearts beat more slowly and they live longer.

West's team argued that the reason is the branching networks inside bodies, arteries and capillaries, which must reach every cell while wasting as little energy as possible.

Cities have networks too: roads, pipes, cables. And they show the same economy of scale. A city twice as big needs only about 85% more petrol stations and road. But here the analogy breaks. A city's social networks, people meeting people, scale the other way, at about 1.15. Bigger cities produce more ideas, wages and crime per person, not less. So where an elephant slows down as it grows, a city **speeds up**. People in bigger cities even walk faster.

The catch, West warns, is that superlinear growth needs ever-faster innovation to avoid collapse. A city is less like an elephant and more like a treadmill that keeps accelerating.

offline_task.title: Test Wirth on your own street
offline_task.body_md:
Take a 20-minute walk through the busiest place near you: a market, a station, a main road. Carry Wirth's three words and Childe's ten traits in your head.

1. **Size:** count how many faces you pass that you recognise. Then estimate how many you do not.
2. **Density:** stop for one minute at a corner and count the people who pass. Multiply by 60 for an hourly figure.
3. **Heterogeneity:** list every different job you see being done (vendor, guard, driver, cook, tailor, delivery rider). Try for 20.
4. **Records:** spot three things that exist only because strangers must trust each other: a receipt, a price board, a QR code, a number plate.

Back home, decide: by Wirth's test, is your neighbourhood a city, a town or a village? Does the official label agree?
